clause: The security deposit of Rs. 1,00,000 paid by the Tenant is non-refundable and shall be forfeited by the Owner under all circumstances upon vacation of the premises.
analysis:
RISK LEVEL: Critical
PLAIN LANGUAGE SUMMARY: This clause means that no matter how carefully you maintain the property or how properly you vacate it, you will permanently lose your entire Rs. 1,00,000 deposit. The landlord can keep it without any justification whatsoever, which is a severe financial loss with no legal backing.
LEGAL ASSESSMENT: This clause is void and unenforceable under Section 23 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, as it is against public policy. Security deposits exist solely to protect the landlord against actual damages or unpaid dues — they cannot be declared non-refundable as a blanket term. No provision of the Maharashtra Rent Control Act, 1999 permits forfeiture of a deposit without proven loss. Any such clause, if challenged before the Court of Small Causes (Mumbai) or Civil Judge (Junior Division) under Section 33, will be struck down.
TENANT ADVISORY: Do not sign this agreement in its current form under any circumstances. Demand the clause be rewritten to read: "The security deposit is refundable, subject only to deductions for actual damages caused by the Tenant beyond normal wear and tear and any unpaid dues." If the landlord refuses to amend this clause, treat it as a serious red flag indicating bad faith. You may approach the District Legal Services Authority (DLSA) for free legal advice before signing.
NEXT STEPS IF ALREADY SIGNED: File a complaint before the Court of Small Causes Mumbai (or Civil Judge Junior Division in other Maharashtra districts) under Section 33 of the Maharashtra Rent Control Act, 1999, seeking recovery of the deposit. The court will treat the non-refundable clause as void. Collect all evidence of the property's condition at vacating — photographs, video, written handover confirmation — to support your claim.

clause: The Licensor shall be entitled to terminate this agreement and recover possession of the premises by giving 24 hours notice to the Licensee in case of any default in payment of rent.
analysis:
RISK LEVEL: Critical
PLAIN LANGUAGE SUMMARY: This clause allows your landlord to evict you with just 24 hours notice if you miss even a single rent payment. This means a one-day delay in paying rent could result in you being forced to vacate your home within a day, which is both practically devastating and legally illegal.
LEGAL ASSESSMENT: This clause directly violates Section 15 of the Maharashtra Rent Control Act, 1999. Under Section 15, a landlord cannot even file a suit for recovery of possession on the ground of non-payment of rent until 90 days have elapsed after serving a written demand notice upon the tenant. Furthermore, even after filing suit, the tenant can avoid eviction by depositing all arrears along with 15% simple interest per annum in court. A 24-hour eviction notice for rent default is therefore legally void and unenforceable.
TENANT ADVISORY: Refuse to sign this clause. The legally valid minimum notice period for rent default under Maharashtra law is 90 days written notice under Section 15. If the landlord insists on retaining this clause, approach the Rent Authority or DLSA before signing.
NEXT STEPS IF LANDLORD ATTEMPTS EVICTION: If your landlord serves a 24-hour eviction notice, do not vacate. Immediately deposit all rent arrears plus 15% interest per annum in the Court of Small Causes (Mumbai) or Civil Judge Junior Division (other areas) under Section 15(3) of the Maharashtra Rent Control Act, 1999. Once you deposit the arrears in court, the landlord cannot obtain an eviction decree against you. Simultaneously send the landlord a registered post letter citing Section 15 and informing them that their notice is legally invalid.

clause: The Landlord or his authorised representatives shall have the right to enter the premises at any time without prior notice for the purpose of inspection, repair or any other reason deemed fit by the Landlord.
analysis:
RISK LEVEL: High
PLAIN LANGUAGE SUMMARY: This clause allows your landlord or anyone he sends to walk into your home at any time, day or night, without warning. This eliminates your right to privacy and peaceful possession — two rights that are legally protected for every tenant in Maharashtra.
LEGAL ASSESSMENT: This clause violates Section 28 of the Maharashtra Rent Control Act, 1999, which explicitly states that a landlord may inspect premises only at a reasonable time and only after giving prior notice to the tenant. "Any time without prior notice" directly contradicts this statutory right. The right to peaceful possession and quiet enjoyment is also a fundamental implied covenant in every tenancy under Indian common law, and a clause attempting to extinguish it is void.
TENANT ADVISORY: Before signing, demand the clause be replaced with: "The Licensor shall have the right to enter and inspect the Licensed premises at a reasonable time, not more than once per month, after giving the Licensee at least 24 hours prior written notice." This is the legally correct formulation consistent with Section 28 of the Act.
NEXT STEPS IF LANDLORD ENTERS WITHOUT NOTICE: Document every unauthorised entry in writing — date, time, what was done — and send the landlord a registered post letter citing Section 28 of the Maharashtra Rent Control Act, 1999, warning that further unauthorised entry will be reported to the Rent Authority and the local police as trespass. If the intrusion continues, file a complaint at the nearest police station under Section 441 of the Indian Penal Code (criminal trespass) and simultaneously approach the Court of Small Causes for an injunction.

clause: The Tenant shall be responsible for all repairs, maintenance, structural alterations and upkeep of the premises including major repairs to walls, plumbing, electrical wiring and roof at his own cost.
analysis:
RISK LEVEL: High
PLAIN LANGUAGE SUMMARY: This clause makes you, the tenant, financially responsible for everything that goes wrong in the property — including structural repairs like broken walls, faulty plumbing, damaged electrical wiring, and roof leaks. These are typically very expensive repairs that can cost tens of thousands of rupees and are not your legal responsibility.
LEGAL ASSESSMENT: This clause violates Section 14 of the Maharashtra Rent Control Act, 1999, which places a clear statutory duty on the landlord to keep the premises in good repair. While minor day-to-day repairs can be assigned to the tenant by agreement, structural and major repairs are the landlord's legal obligation and cannot be contractually shifted to the tenant. Any clause attempting to do so is unenforceable. Specifically, Section 14 allows a tenant to carry out repairs the landlord neglects and deduct the cost from rent after serving 15 days written notice — this right cannot be waived by contract.
TENANT ADVISORY: Negotiate this clause down to minor repairs only — for example, "The Licensee shall be responsible for minor day-to-day repairs not exceeding Rs. 500 per incident." Add an explicit line: "All structural repairs, major plumbing, electrical rewiring and roof repairs shall remain the sole responsibility of the Licensor, consistent with Section 14 of the Maharashtra Rent Control Act, 1999."
NEXT STEPS IF LANDLORD REFUSES MAJOR REPAIRS: Serve the landlord a formal written notice (by registered post) specifying the repair required and giving 15 days to complete it, as required by Section 14 of the Maharashtra Rent Control Act, 1999. If the landlord does not act within 15 days, you are legally entitled to carry out the repair yourself and deduct the full cost from your next rent payment. Keep all receipts and document the repair with photographs.

clause: In the event of any dispute arising out of this agreement, the matter shall be referred to arbitration and the decision of the arbitrator appointed by the Landlord shall be final and binding on both parties.
analysis:
RISK LEVEL: High
PLAIN LANGUAGE SUMMARY: This clause forces you to resolve all disputes through an arbitrator personally chosen by your landlord, and makes that arbitrator's decision final and unchallengeable. This means the person deciding your case is effectively appointed and paid by the other side, completely eliminating any possibility of a fair hearing.
LEGAL ASSESSMENT: Under Section 33 of the Maharashtra Rent Control Act, 1999, disputes between landlord and tenant relating to recovery of rent, possession, and other tenancy matters fall exclusively within the jurisdiction of the Court of Small Causes (in Brihan Mumbai) or the Court of Civil Judge Junior Division (in other Maharashtra areas). These statutory jurisdictions cannot be contractually ousted by an arbitration clause. Furthermore, an arbitration clause where only one party appoints the arbitrator violates the fundamental principle of natural justice and would be void under Section 12 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, which requires arbitrators to be independent and impartial.
TENANT ADVISORY: Refuse this clause entirely. Insist it be replaced with: "Any dispute arising out of this agreement shall be resolved in accordance with the Maharashtra Rent Control Act, 1999, before the Court of Small Causes, Mumbai (or the Civil Judge Junior Division for other Maharashtra areas) as specified under Section 33 of the said Act."
NEXT STEPS IF LANDLORD INVOKES THIS CLAUSE: Do not participate in any arbitration proceeding conducted by a landlord-appointed arbitrator. Instead, directly approach the Court of Small Causes (Mumbai) or Civil Judge Junior Division (other areas) under Section 33 of the Maharashtra Rent Control Act, 1999. File a written objection stating that the arbitration clause is void as it attempts to oust statutory jurisdiction. The court will hear your matter regardless of the arbitration clause.

clause: The Licensor reserves the right to increase the monthly rent by any amount at any time during the subsistence of this agreement by giving 7 days notice to the Licensee.
analysis:
RISK LEVEL: High
PLAIN LANGUAGE SUMMARY: This clause gives your landlord the right to raise your rent by any amount — even doubling or tripling it — at any point during your tenancy, with just 7 days notice. This makes your housing cost completely unpredictable and could force you out of your home if you cannot afford the sudden increase.
LEGAL ASSESSMENT: This clause violates the rent increase limits prescribed under the Maharashtra Rent Control Act, 1999. Under Section 11 of the Act, a landlord is entitled to increase rent by a maximum of 4% per annum for residential, educational, commercial and storage premises. An additional increase of up to 15% per annum is permitted only for expenses on special alterations or additional amenities actually provided. Any rent increase beyond these statutory limits is illegal and unenforceable. The 7-day notice period is also grossly inadequate — any increase should be prospective and clearly documented.
TENANT ADVISORY: Before signing, demand this clause be amended to read: "The monthly compensation shall not be increased by more than 4% per annum as permitted under Section 11 of the Maharashtra Rent Control Act, 1999, with a minimum of 30 days prior written notice." Do not accept open-ended rent revision clauses under any circumstances.
NEXT STEPS IF LANDLORD DEMANDS EXCESS INCREASE: Refuse to pay any increase beyond 4% per annum. Send the landlord a registered post letter citing Section 11 of the Maharashtra Rent Control Act, 1999, and stating the legally permissible increase amount. If the landlord threatens eviction for non-payment of the excess amount, approach the Court of Small Causes (Mumbai) or Civil Judge Junior Division and apply under Section 8 for the court to fix the standard rent. Note that charging rent in excess of the standard rent is a criminal offence under Section 10 of the Act, punishable with imprisonment up to 3 months or a fine up to Rs. 5,000 or both.

clause: The Landlord shall not be responsible for providing or maintaining any essential services including water supply, electricity connection, lift, or sanitation to the premises.
analysis:
RISK LEVEL: Critical
PLAIN LANGUAGE SUMMARY: This clause says your landlord has no obligation to ensure you have water, electricity, a working lift, or sanitation. If any of these are cut off or stopped working, the landlord can simply refuse to fix them and point to this clause as justification.
LEGAL ASSESSMENT: This clause directly violates Section 29 of the Maharashtra Rent Control Act, 1999, which expressly prohibits a landlord from cutting off or withholding any essential supply or service — including water, electricity, lighting in passages and staircases, lifts, and sanitation. A contractual clause cannot override this statutory prohibition. Violation of Section 29 is a cognizable criminal offence under Section 53 of the Act, attracting a fine of Rs. 100 per day for each day of default, and continued failure to restore essential services after a court order attracts imprisonment up to 3 months or a fine up to Rs. 1,000 or both.
TENANT ADVISORY: This clause is void on its face and cannot be enforced against you regardless of the fact that you signed the agreement containing it. However, you should demand it be struck from the agreement before signing. Add a replacement clause: "The Licensor shall ensure the continuous provision of all essential services to the Licensed Premises including water, electricity and lift, in accordance with Section 29 of the Maharashtra Rent Control Act, 1999."
NEXT STEPS IF ESSENTIAL SERVICES ARE CUT: If your landlord cuts water, electricity, or any other essential service, approach the Court of Small Causes (Mumbai) or Civil Judge Junior Division immediately under Section 29(2) of the Maharashtra Rent Control Act, 1999. The court can issue an interim order restoring the service within days. Simultaneously file a police complaint as this is a cognizable offence under Section 53. Document the disruption with dated photographs and written communication to the landlord.

clause: The Tenant shall vacate the premises immediately upon verbal or written notice from the Owner for any reason the Owner deems fit, without any right to contest or seek legal remedy.
analysis:
RISK LEVEL: Critical
PLAIN LANGUAGE SUMMARY: This clause claims that your landlord can tell you to leave your home at any time, for any reason, and that you have no right to challenge this or go to court. This is one of the most dangerous clauses a rental agreement can contain — it attempts to strip you of all legal protection as a tenant.
LEGAL ASSESSMENT: This clause is completely void under Indian law. Under Section 16 of the Maharashtra Rent Control Act, 1999, a landlord can only recover possession of tenanted premises on specific exhaustive grounds listed in the section — including damage to property, illegal subletting, non-payment of rent, or bona fide personal requirement. An arbitrary "any reason" eviction clause has no legal standing. Furthermore, Section 15 requires 90 days written notice before a suit for non-payment eviction can even be filed. The phrase "without any right to contest or seek legal remedy" is void under Article 21 of the Constitution of India, which guarantees the right to approach courts for legal redress. No private contract can waive constitutional rights.
TENANT ADVISORY: Refuse to sign this clause without exception. This clause attempts to make you legally defenceless and has no place in any legitimate rental agreement. Its presence in the agreement is itself a serious indicator of bad faith by the landlord.
NEXT STEPS IF LANDLORD ATTEMPTS EVICTION UNDER THIS CLAUSE: Do not vacate. Immediately consult a lawyer or approach the District Legal Services Authority for free legal aid. File a suit in the Court of Small Causes (Mumbai) or Civil Judge Junior Division under Section 33 of the Maharashtra Rent Control Act, 1999, seeking an injunction against eviction and a declaration that the clause is void. The court will protect your possession while the matter is being heard. If the landlord attempts physical eviction, file a police complaint for wrongful eviction and criminal trespass under the Indian Penal Code.

clause: The Licensee shall pay stamp duty, registration charges, legal fees and all incidental costs for the execution and registration of this Leave and License Agreement.
analysis:
RISK LEVEL: High
PLAIN LANGUAGE SUMMARY: This clause makes you, the tenant, pay all the costs of getting the agreement legally registered — including stamp duty, registration fees, and lawyer charges. In Maharashtra, stamp duty on rental agreements is calculated as a percentage of total rent plus deposit and can run into thousands of rupees. This is a cost the law says the landlord must bear.
LEGAL ASSESSMENT: This clause violates Section 55 of the Maharashtra Rent Control Act, 1999, which places the obligation of executing a written agreement and getting it registered squarely on the Licensor (landlord). The landlord's failure to register a Leave and License agreement is a criminal offence under Section 55(3), punishable with imprisonment up to 3 months or a fine up to Rs. 5,000 or both. Shifting this statutory obligation and its associated costs to the tenant via a private clause is legally impermissible. However, it is worth noting that an unregistered agreement does not protect the tenant's right to possession before the Rent Court — so registration is in your interest too.
TENANT ADVISORY: Demand that this clause be amended to place the cost of registration on the Licensor as required by Section 55 of the Maharashtra Rent Control Act, 1999. While you may choose to voluntarily contribute to registration costs as a commercial matter, you should never be contractually obligated to bear them. Ensure the agreement is registered regardless of who pays — an unregistered agreement is unreliable as evidence in court.
NEXT STEPS IF LANDLORD REFUSES TO REGISTER: Report the landlord's failure to register the agreement to the Sub-Registrar of Assurances in your area. You may also file a complaint under Section 55(3) of the Maharashtra Rent Control Act, 1999, which makes failure to register a cognizable offence. Keep all payment receipts and WhatsApp or written communications as documentary evidence of your tenancy even if the agreement is unregistered.

clause: If the Licensee fails to vacate the premises on the expiry of the license period, the Licensor shall be entitled to disconnect electricity and water supply and remove the Licensee's belongings from the premises without any court order.
analysis:
RISK LEVEL: Critical
PLAIN LANGUAGE SUMMARY: This clause says that if you do not leave exactly on time, your landlord can immediately cut off your electricity and water and physically remove all your belongings without going to court first. This is essentially a threat of vigilante eviction written into the agreement.
LEGAL ASSESSMENT: This clause violates two separate provisions of the Maharashtra Rent Control Act, 1999. First, cutting off electricity and water supply violates Section 29, which prohibits withholding essential services, a cognizable criminal offence under Section 53 attracting fines of Rs. 100 per day and potential imprisonment. Second, removing a tenant's belongings without a court order constitutes wrongful eviction — there is no provision in Indian law permitting self-help eviction. The proper legal remedy for the landlord is to apply to the competent authority under Section 24 of the Act, which will pass an eviction order after satisfying itself of the expiry of the license period.
TENANT ADVISORY: This clause is void and cannot be legally enforced even if you have signed it. However, do not rely on its voidness alone — demand it be struck from the agreement before signing. Add a clause stating: "Upon expiry of the license period, recovery of possession shall be governed by Section 24 of the Maharashtra Rent Control Act, 1999, through the appropriate competent authority."
NEXT STEPS IF LANDLORD CUTS SERVICES OR REMOVES BELONGINGS: Immediately call the police and file a complaint for criminal trespass and theft of belongings under the Indian Penal Code. Simultaneously approach the Court of Small Causes (Mumbai) or Civil Judge Junior Division under Section 29(2) of the Maharashtra Rent Control Act, 1999, for immediate restoration of essential services. File a separate application for an injunction restraining the landlord from interfering with your possession. Document all incidents with photographs, videos, and written communication.

Licensee/s shall maintain premises in existing condition. 6) No alteration without written consent. 7) No tenancy right, no subletting, no mortgage. 8) Licensor has right of access on reasonable notice at reasonable intervals. 9) Default in payment: Licensor entitled to revoke by giving one month notice. Licensee can vacate by one month notice. 10) On expiration Licensee shall vacate. Failure to vacate: damages at double daily rate or Licensor entitled to remove Licensee without recourse to Court of Law. 12) This Agreement is to be registered and expenditure of Stamp duty and registration fees shall be borne by the Licensor/s.
analysis:
### 📋 OVERALL CONTRACT SUMMARY
This is the official IGR Maharashtra government template for a Leave and License Agreement issued under Section 24 of the Maharashtra Rent Control Act, 1999. The agreement is largely balanced and the registration costs are correctly placed on the Licensor. However, it contains two Critical risks that every tenant must address before signing: the non-refundable deposit option in Clause 2.3, and the self-help eviction provision in Clause 10. If the landlord selects the non-refundable deposit variant or invokes the no-court-order eviction clause, the tenant faces severe financial and personal risk.

### ✅ THE GOOD (Fair Clauses)
* Clause 9 grants both parties equal one-month written notice rights for cancellation, ensuring neither party can be abruptly displaced. This is consistent with the protections under Section 24 of the Maharashtra Rent Control Act, 1999, and represents a fair balance of rights.
* Clause 12 correctly places the burden of stamp duty, registration fees, and incidental charges on the Licensor. This is the legally mandated position under Section 55 of the Maharashtra Rent Control Act, 1999, and protects the tenant from being illegally charged these costs.
* Clause 3(b) provides a legally sound refundable deposit mechanism — the deposit is returned at vacation with deductions only for legitimate outstanding dues. This is consistent with tenant protection principles under Indian contract law.

### ❌ THE BAD (High Risks)
* Clause 2.3 offers a non-refundable deposit/premium option. If the landlord selects this variant, the tenant permanently forfeits their entire deposit regardless of the condition in which they leave the property. This is void under Section 23 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, and has no backing in the Maharashtra Rent Control Act, 1999.
* Clause 10 states the Licensor may remove the Licensee and belongings "without recourse to the Court of Law" if the Licensee fails to vacate on time. Self-help eviction is illegal under Indian law. The landlord's correct remedy is applying to the competent authority under Section 24 of the Maharashtra Rent Control Act, 1999. Cutting services to force eviction additionally violates Section 29 of the Act.

### ⚠️ MIGHT BE A PROBLEM (Gray Areas)
* Clause 4 presents two maintenance options without requiring one to be struck off. If Clause 4.2 is selected, the tenant bears all maintenance charges with no monetary cap or definition of scope. Without limits, this could include building fund contributions, sinking fund levies, and other society charges the tenant never anticipated.

---
### 🔍 DETAILED CLAUSE ANALYSIS

**CLAUSE 1:** "That the Licensee/s shall pay to the Licensor/s towards the compensation and Rs non-refundable deposit/premium for the use of the said Licenced premises."
**RISK LEVEL:** Critical
**PLAIN LANGUAGE SUMMARY:** If the landlord selects this clause variant, you permanently lose your entire deposit when you vacate — regardless of the property's condition, regardless of whether you paid all rent on time, and regardless of any other circumstance. There is no legal basis for this whatsoever.
**LEGAL ASSESSMENT:** A non-refundable security deposit is void under Section 23 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, as it is against public policy. Security deposits exist solely to protect against actual damages or unpaid dues and must be refunded upon vacation subject only to legitimate deductions. This clause will be struck down if challenged before the Court of Small Causes Mumbai or Civil Judge Junior Division under Section 33 of the Maharashtra Rent Control Act, 1999.
**TENANT ADVISORY:** Refuse to sign the agreement if Clause 2.3 is selected. Insist only on Clause 2.2 — interest-free refundable deposit. If the landlord refuses, approach the District Legal Services Authority for free legal advice before proceeding.
**NEXT STEPS IF DEPOSIT IS WITHHELD:** File a recovery suit before the Court of Small Causes Mumbai (or Civil Judge Junior Division elsewhere) under Section 33 of the Maharashtra Rent Control Act, 1999. The non-refundable clause will be declared void and the court will order full refund. Bring all documentation: the signed agreement, proof of payment, photographs of the property at vacation, and written handover communication.

**CLAUSE 2:** "The Licensor shall be entitled to remove the Licensee and his/her/their belongings from the Licenced premises, without recourse to the Court of Law."
**RISK LEVEL:** Critical
**PLAIN LANGUAGE SUMMARY:** This clause claims the landlord can physically throw you and your belongings out of your home without a court order if you do not vacate on time. In practice this means changed locks, removed furniture, and no legal recourse according to the agreement — all of which is false.
**LEGAL ASSESSMENT:** Self-help eviction without a court order is illegal under Indian law regardless of what a private agreement states. The proper remedy is for the landlord to apply to the competent authority under Section 24 of the Maharashtra Rent Control Act, 1999, which will pass an eviction order after verifying expiry of the license. If the landlord also cuts essential services to force eviction, that is a separate cognizable criminal offence under Section 29 read with Section 53 of the Act, attracting fines of Rs. 100 per day and imprisonment up to 3 months.
**TENANT ADVISORY:** Note that this clause cannot be legally enforced against you. However, insist on its deletion before signing and replace it with: "Recovery of possession upon expiry shall be governed by Section 24 of the Maharashtra Rent Control Act, 1999."
**NEXT STEPS IF LANDLORD ATTEMPTS SELF-HELP EVICTION:** Do not vacate under duress. Call the police immediately and file a complaint for criminal trespass under the Indian Penal Code. File an application before the Court of Small Causes Mumbai or Civil Judge Junior Division for an injunction restraining the landlord from interfering with your possession. If essential services are cut, file a separate urgent application under Section 29(2) of the Maharashtra Rent Control Act, 1999 — courts typically issue interim restoration orders within days.

**CLAUSE 3:** "That the Licensee/s herein shall bear and pay all the maintenance charges in respect of the said Licenced Premises."
**RISK LEVEL:** Medium
**PLAIN LANGUAGE SUMMARY:** You will pay all maintenance charges for the property, but the agreement does not define what these charges include or set any limit on the amount. The landlord could present you with unexpected charges — like building fund contributions or sinking fund levies — that you never discussed.
**LEGAL ASSESSMENT:** Assigning maintenance to the licensee is legally permissible under a Leave and License Agreement. However, the absence of a definition or cap makes this clause vague and potentially exploitative. Under Section 14 of the Maharashtra Rent Control Act, 1999, structural repairs and major building maintenance remain the Licensor's statutory responsibility regardless of any contractual clause to the contrary.
**TENANT ADVISORY:** Before signing, request the last three months of society maintenance bills to understand the actual monthly cost. Negotiate a written cap on your maintenance liability and explicitly exclude structural repairs, building fund, and sinking fund contributions from your responsibility.
**NEXT STEPS IF OVERCHARGED:** If the landlord demands maintenance charges beyond what was agreed or charges you for structural repairs, send a written objection by registered post citing Section 14 of the Maharashtra Rent Control Act, 1999. Retain all maintenance payment receipts to protect against deposit deduction claims at vacation.

However, two clauses create significant risk: the undefined maintenance cost structure (Clauses 3 and 4) creates unpredictable monthly financial obligations, and Clause 21 illegally shifts 50% of the stamp duty burden to the tenant. ### ✅ THE GOOD (Fair Clauses)
* Clause 6 contains an exceptionally strong tenant protection: if the Owner fails to refund the security deposit upon termination, the Tenant is legally entitled to continue occupying the premises rent-free until the deposit is returned. This direct remedy is rarely seen in standard agreements and provides strong leverage against landlords who withhold deposits.
* Clause 11 limits the Owner's right to inspect the premises to once per month, consistent with the reasonable notice requirement under Section 28 of the Maharashtra Rent Control Act, 1999. This protects the tenant's right to peaceful possession.

### ❌ THE BAD (High Risks)
* Clauses 3 and 4 together impose a fixed maintenance charge plus a completely undefined variable running cost for the elevator and generator. With no cap on the variable cost, the tenant's total monthly financial obligation is unpredictable and entirely at the landlord's discretion. This is a significant financial risk dressed up as a routine clause.
* Clause 21 requires the tenant to pay 50% of stamp duty and registration costs. This contradicts Section 55 of the Maharashtra Rent Control Act, 1999, which places the legal obligation of registration on the Licensor. Shifting 50% of this cost to the tenant has no statutory backing and is financially unfair.

* Clause 20 refers to the jurisdiction of "the (city) civil courts" without specifying the city or the correct court. Under Section 33 of the Maharashtra Rent Control Act, 1999, disputes in Brihan Mumbai must go before the Court of Small Causes, not general civil courts. This blank creates potential for the landlord to claim a favourable or inconvenient jurisdiction later.

---
### 🔍 DETAILED CLAUSE ANALYSIS

**CLAUSE 1:** "Tenant shall pay monthly maintenance charge of Rs.(Amount) towards Generator, Elevator, guards, Common Area electricity. Tenant shall pay running cost of elevator and generator separately."

**PLAIN LANGUAGE SUMMARY:** You pay two separate charges on top of rent — a fixed maintenance amount plus a variable running cost for the elevator and generator that has no upper limit.
